title: ANSPDCP (Romania) - Fine against a sole trader acting as a controller
text:
English Summary[edit | edit source]
Facts[edit | edit source]
A sole trader providing transport services through a ride-hailing platform (controller) disclosed a client’s (data subject) identity, image, ride and location data on social media.
Following a complaint, the DPA launched an investigation into this disclosure.

Holding[edit | edit source]
The DPA found that the controller disclosed the data subject’s personal data on social media without consent or another legal basis, in breach of Article 6(1) GDPR.
Consequently, the DPA fined the controller €1,000 (RON 5,265) for this violation.
The controller subsequently paid the fine imposed.

title: IMY (Sweden) - IMY-2025-11707
text:
English Summary[edit | edit source]
Facts[edit | edit source]
The DPA received multiple complaints about Nusvar AB (the controller) which provides a search service on a website. Particularly, these requests addressed the controllers inadequate handling of erasure requests from data subjects.
In its defence, the controller exemplified that the GDPR and the national Data Protection Act are not applicable to it. Specifically, because the processing of personal data by the controller was intended for journalistic purposes and thus subject to the Freedom of the Press Act.
The controller further explained that the purpose of the service is to inform the public and that it serves as a third-party tool for both local and national newsrooms. In that regard, the controller explained that all publications undergo a privacy assessment and anything which falls outside the controller’s journalistic purpose or violates applicable law under the Freedom of the Press Act is removed.
Moreover, the controller stated that according to the GDPR and Freedom of the Press Act, databases containing voluntary disclosure statements are not within the scope of Article 17 GDPR. Regardless, the controller informed that they have internal policies which allow for personal data erasure, however without a review of the specific circumstances.
Since the DPA initiated its investigation and brought the matter to the attention of the controller, the controller erased the personal data of the data subjects concerned.

Holding[edit | edit source]
Primarily, the DPA held that the mere fact that journalists may use the database in their journalistic work does not mean that the service is operated specifically for journalistic purposes. Particularly because the controller provides and makes available an extensive collection of personal data from public sources without distinction. In light of the CJEU's established criteria for journalistic purposes, the DPA held that the controller’s processing operations did not intend to disseminate information, opinions, or ideas to the public and thus could not be considered to fulfill a journalistic purpose.
Furthermore, regarding the data subjects’ requests for erasure, the DPA maintained the controller’s obligation to erase the personal data of a data subject upon their request, unless the controller is able to demonstrate the applicability of an exception (Article 17 GDPR).
In light of this, the DPA held that the controller did not assess the reasons of the data subjects request and neither did it consider the exception concerning the right to freedom of expression and information of Article 17(3) GDPR.
As a result, the DPA found the controller to have conducted personal data processing in violation of Article 17(1) GDPR. Correspondingly, the DPA reprimanded the controller pursuant to Article 58(2)(b) GDPR.

title: IMY (Sweden) - IMY-2025-6465
text:
English Summary[edit | edit source]
Facts[edit | edit source]
The DPA received multiple complaints from data subjects concerning the processing of personal data relating to criminal offenses by Fuplex AB (the controller) on its search service.
The website had been active since 2022, comprised a collection of court rulings from 2018 onwards and preliminary investigation records from 2019, from all of Sweden’s courts from the past five years, after five years they are automatically purged. The documents are uploaded and individuals may download them in a PDF format. Website visitors are able to search for individuals who have been defendants by name, address and personal identification number and can obtain access to articles and audio files from trials.
During the investigation, the controller informed about its publication certificate, granted pursuant to the Freedom of the Press Act, enshrining its responsibility to process personal data. This certificate also means that the processing and publication of materials are protected by the constitution. The controller further clarified that where the GDPR and national Data Protection Act conflict with the Freedom of the Press Act the former two shall not apply.
The controller claimed that its activities constitute journalistic purposes and emphasised that where the controller is conducting its business activities, the GDPR does not apply to the personal data relating to criminal convictions and offences.

Holding[edit | edit source]
Primarily, whilst the controller claimed that it was fulfilling a journalistic purpose in, the DPA held otherwise. The DPA noted the large number of judgements and preliminary investigation records which were made available in a searchable form, and the number of documents which contained personal data relating to criminal offences.
Following the CJEU in ND v Legal Newsdesk Sweden AB (C-199/24) where the assessment criteria for journalistic purposes was established, the DPA held that the controller’s processing operations did not intend to disseminate information, opinions, or ideas to the public and thus could not be considered to fulfil a journalistic purpose.
Furthermore, the DPA placed particular importance on the nature of the data processed by the controller, particularly of personal data related to criminal offences. The DPA emphasised the applicability of Article 10 GDPR and the necessity to fulfil the requirement (authorised by national or EU law) which would allow for such processing.
The DPA found that the controller did not demonstrate that it has a legal basis as required by Article 10 GDPR and that the controller processed personal data related to criminal convictions and offenses in violation of that provision.
Pursuant to Article 58(2)(b) GDPR the DPA issued a reprimand against the controller.

title: Garante per la protezione dei dati personali (Italy) - 10309500-n.761
text:
English Summary[edit | edit source]
Facts[edit | edit source]
The Italian Ministry of Justice (the controller) organised a public examination for admission to the notary profession. After the written examinations, the controller placed a list containing the results of the people participating in the examination (the data subjects) on a table in the Ministry's entrance hall, before the security gates, where it was accessible to anyone. 
The list contained the personal data of 1,229 successful and unsuccessful candidates. It included, among others, their names, date of birth, and their test scores. 
The applicable national law required the controller to display, at the door of the examination room, a list containing only the names of candidates admitted to the next stage of the examination. 
The Italian DPA learned from this processing due to various news articles on this practice. 


Holding[edit | edit source]
The DPA held that public authorities could process personal data when necessary to comply with a legal obligation or perform a task in the public interest under Article 6(1)(c) or (e) GDPR and that under Article 6(2) and (3) GDPR, the legal basis should be laid down in national or EU law. The applicable national law authorised the publication of names of candidates admitted to the oral examination but not the disclosure of personal data of unsuccessful candidates. Therefore, the controller made the personal data of data subjects available without a legal basis. 
The DPA also held that candidates' date of birth and examination scores were not necessary to announce which candidates had been successful. Therefore, the controller infringed the principle of lawfulness, fairness and transparency (Article 5(1)(a) GDPR) and the principle of data minimisation (Article 5(1)(c) GDPR) . 
The DPA fined the Ministry of Justice €20.000.

title: Hoge Raad - 25/02752
text:
English Summary[edit | edit source]
Facts[edit | edit source]
In 2022, ING (the controller) ended the banking relationship of a client (data subject) for not giving a transparent picture of the use of his business account in a periodic client survey. Therefore, the data subject was not able to provide enough information to fulfil the obligations under the Financial Supervision Act (Wet Financieel Toezicht) and the Law on the Prevention of Money Laundering and the Financing of Terrorism (Wwft). The controller noted down in their event administration and internal register that there were too large cash expenditures and the inadequate accounting thereof, and that too few measures were taken to exclude its involvement in handling stolen goods, money laundering, and other financial economic crimes. This data is retained for a period of 8 years.
In front of the court, the data subject ordered the controller to delete his data in its registers, in order that it no longer gives the impression that he is involved in or that there could be a risk of being involved in a crime. The court rejected his claim. The data subject appealed, ordering the controller to erase all personal data in the administration from which it follows that it cannot be excluded that he has committed money laundering or any other form of crime, and to delete the registration in the internal register.
On appeal, the data subject argued this registration should be regarded as the registration of personal data under Article 10 GDPR, and should require the high standard of ‘more than a reasonable suspicion of guilt’. The court of appeal rejected this claim by stating that criminal personal data needs to be such concrete facts and circumstances that it qualifies as a criminal offence under the Dutch Code of Criminal Procedure, thus not just a statement stating the facts around the large cash expenditures. By referencing to their code of conduct, the controller stated that they use the legal basis of legitimate interests under Article 6(1)(f) GDPR to ensure the security and integrity of the financial sector, and that this data was never accessible to third-parties. In conclusion, the court of appeal upheld this rejection and held that the registration only mentioned the reason of the termination of the banking relationship.
The data subject appealed this to the Supreme Court. 


Holding[edit | edit source]
In his first claim, the data subject argued the court of appeal failed to recognise the autonomous meaning in the EU of ‘criminal offence’ under Article 10 GDPR. The Supreme Court confirmed that this autonomous meaning needs to be applied, and referenced to CJEU B/Latvijas Republikas Saei (C-439/19) in which there are three criteria to assess whether a ‘criminal offence’ has a criminal nature. The three criteria are: (i) the legal classification of the offence under national law, (ii) the nature itself of the offence, and (iii) the gravity of the penalty that may be imposed on the data subject. The Supreme Court defined in 2009 ‘criminal personal data’ as concrete facts or circumstances that can prove a criminal offence and this data must be sufficiently established, meaning there is more than just a reasonable suspicion of guilt. During the party debate, the court of appeal ruled that the second and third criteria did not apply, thus it ruled there was no criminal personal data based off the legal classification under national law. Therefore, the Supreme Court dismissed this claim stating the court did not misunderstood this autonomous meaning.
In his second claim, the data subject argued the court of appeal failed to recognise that the controller should cease the processing of personal data based on Article 21(1) GDPR, unless it provides compelling legitimate grounds for the processing that outweigh the ones of the data subject. In his opinion the court of appeal wrongly failed to investigate the existence of those legitimate grounds. The Supreme Court held that the controller has a compelling legitimate interest, since the controller needs to fulfil its obligations under the Law on the Prevention of Money Laundering and the Financing of Terrorism (Wwft). Therefore, the Supreme Court dismissed this claim, stating the court of appeal already came to this conclusion.
In conclusion, the Supreme Court the appeal.

title: AEPD (Spain) - PS/00377/2025
text:
English Summary[edit | edit source]
Facts[edit | edit source]
The DPA received a complaint by a data subject after a controller created fake profiles in the data subjects name, and published images from eight years ago where the data subject appeared naked. The images were published and made available on multiple websites.
The DPA initiated a preliminary investigation, and located links and images of the data subject on other websites. The DPA found the data subject and the images in question on 89 websites. The DPA contacted some of the websites and requested them to remove the images, however on eight websites removal did not happen.

Holding[edit | edit source]
The DPA held that in the present case, numerous images of the data subject were published on various websites which constitutes processing of personal data by the controller. The images contained erotic or pornographic content and included the data subjects face and naked body, making her clearly recognizable and identifiable. The DPA held that the controller was unable to sufficiently demonstrate that one of the legal bases of Article 6 GDPR were applicable to the personal data processing of the data subject.
As a result, the DPA held that the controller was in violation of Article 6 GDPR. The fine was initially set at €10,000 but pursuant to Law 39/2015, a Spanish law concerning administrative proceedings, the DPA informed the controller that it may make a voluntary payment of the proposed fine and waive their right to appeal. This action reduces the imposed fine by 20%. The fine can be reduced by a further 20% if the controller acknowledges its liability. The controller opted for both and reduced the fine by 40%, paying the reduced sanction amount of €6,000.

title: US Zagreb - Us I-3380/2025-9
text:
English Summary[edit | edit source]
Facts[edit | edit source]
A fast-food franchise company operating Pizza Hut restaurants in Croatia (the controller), published a privacy policy on its website informing users that they could exercise their data protection rights either by email at a designated email address or by post to its registered office.
On 12 May 2025, an individual (the data subject) sent an access request under Article 15 GDPR to the designated email address, seeking confirmation and information regarding all personal data processed about them. The data subject immediately received an automated error response indicating that the controller’s email address was not found or was unable to receive emails.
On 16 May 2025, the data subject lodged a complaint with the Croatian Personal Data Protection Agency (the DPA), enclosing copies of the sent email and the delivery failure notification.
On 6 August 2025, the DPA issued a decision finding that the controller breached Article 12(1) in conjunction with Article 15 GDPR by failing to implement appropriate measures to enable electronic communication for the exercise of data subject rights. The DPA noted that controllers must facilitate the exercise of data subject rights pursuant to Article 12(1) and Article 12(2), that pointing the data subject to postal mail was insufficient, and that the controller failed to prove the email system was functioning under Article 5(2) GDPR.
On 9 September 2025, the controller challenged the DPA’s decision before the Administrative Court in Zagreb (the court), seeking its annulment.
The controller argued that it had never collected or processed any personal data relating to the particular data subject, meaning the latter could not be considered a "data subject" within the meaning of the GDPR nor could the controller be considered a "controller" in that regard. Furthermore, according to the controller, the DPA failed to establish or provide evidence that any processing of the data subject’s data had occurred. The controller also argued that its email system operated continuously and properly, proposing that an IT forensic expert examination be conducted on these circumstances.
The DPA maintained that any individual is entitled to request access to ascertain whether their data is being processed, and that the burden of proving that the email system was operational rested on the controller.

Holding[edit | edit source]
The court dismissed the controller’s claim and upheld the decision of the DPA.
First, the court dismissed the controller’s argument that the particular data subject could not be considered a "data subject" within the meaning of the GDPR and that the controller was not a "controller" because the data subject’s data had never been processed by it. The court pointed out that every individual has a fundamental right to request confirmation as to whether a controller processes their personal data. Therefore, the court held that the right of access applies equally when no personal data of the concerned data subject is processed, requiring the controller to respond and confirm in that case that it does not process the data subject’s data. 
Second, the court held that the controller breached its obligation to provide modalities that facilitate the exercise of data subject rights by failing to ensure that its designated email address for data subject communications was operational.
Third, the court rejected the controller’s defence that the data subject could have exercised their right by sending a postal letter to its registered office. The court held that referring the data subject exclusively to postal communications imposes an additional financial burden on the data subject in the form of postage fees.
Fourth, the court held that the burden of proving that the designated email address was active and functioning rested on the controller. 
Consequently, the court upheld the DPA’s finding of an infringement of Article 12(1) and Article 15 GDPR.

title: VDAI (Lithuania) - 3R-(2.13-1E)
text:
English Summary[edit | edit source]
Facts[edit | edit source]
In 2024, a data subject requested the deletion of his account on Vinted (controller), after it was blocked due to violations of the platform’s rules. The controller rejected this request, stating that the request lacks the grounds necessary to exercise the right to erasure under Article 17 GDPR.
According to prior statements to the DPA, after blocking an account, all available data of the data subject is being processed and retained for 3 months. The controller claims it has a legitimate interest under Article 6(1)(f) GDPR in order to ensure a blocked user does not take advantage of being able to re-register on the platform. 
The data subject lodged a complaint in front of the Polish DPA, claiming the controller refused to act upon his request. The Lithuanian DPA, as the lead supervisory authority, took over this complaint.


Holding[edit | edit source]
The DPA held that the controller did act upon the request of the data subject, by providing a statement after the request was made. Additionally, it held that the erasure of personal data was not required, since none of the grounds under Article 17(1) GDPR were applicable and the controller had a legal basis for processing the data under Article 6 GDPR. Therefore, the DPA dismissed this part of the claim.
Furthermore, the DPA examined the quality of the action of the controller upon the request. It found that the controller acted in a non-transparent and unfair manner toward the data subject.
First, it referred to the EDPB Guidelines 01/2024 and 01/2022, and stated the controller has an obligation to actively communicate with the data subject.[1] The controller did not ask for additional information about the personal data to be provided by the data subject.
Second, the controller has an obligation to inform the data subject, using clear and plain language, that it fulfilled its obligation in analysing all circumstances under which Article 17(1) GDPR could be applicable. Solely stating that the request lacks the grounds necessary to exercise the right to erasure, shifted the burden of proof.
Third, according to the prior statements of the controller, other purposes and other legal bases were present upon which it retains the data, besides Article 6(1)(f) GDPR to avoid re-registration on the platform. The controller did not inform the data subject about the existence of these specific purposes, which is an obligation under Article 12(4) GDPR. This could lead to the risk of the data subject being deprived from taking well-founded legal action.
Therefore, the controller violated Article 5(1)(a) and Article 12(1) and (4) GDPR. Since the account of the data subject had already been deleted, and the controller had already been sanctioned and fined in prior decisions regarding the same violations, the DPA did not impose any new sanctions.


↑ https://www.edpb.europa.eu/public-consultations/guidelines-12024-on-processing-of-personal-data-based-on-article-61f-gdpr_en & https://www.edpb.europa.eu/documents/guideline/guidelines-012022-on-data-subject-rights-right-of-access_en

title: ANSPDCP (Romania) - HORA CREDIT IFN S.A
text:
English Summary[edit | edit source]
Facts[edit | edit source]
Hora Credit IFN S.A., a non-banking financial institution (the controller), suffered a cyberattack on its IT infrastructure. The incident compromised the confidentiality, integrity, and security of personal data belonging to a very large number of individuals, including current and former clients, employees, and collaborators (the data subjects). As a result of the breach, unauthorized access was gained to the data subjects' personal information stored within the controller's operational records, electronic correspondence, and contractual documents. Following the incident, the controller submitted a data breach notification to the Romanian Data Protection Authority (DPA) in accordance with Article 33 GDPR. This notification subsequently prompted the DPA to launch an investigation into the controller's data security practices.


Holding[edit | edit source]
First, the DPA held that the controller violated [[Article 32 GDPR#1b]] and [[Article 32 GDPR#2]] by failing to implement adequate technical and organizational measures. The DPA found that the controller did not regularly test, assess, and evaluate the effectiveness of its security measures to ensure a level of security appropriate to the risk, including the ongoing confidentiality, integrity, availability, and resilience of its processing systems.
Second, the DPA considered that these security failures facilitated a cyberattack on the controller's IT infrastructure. This incident resulted in unauthorized access to the personal data of a very large number of data subjects, including clients, employees, and collaborators, and compromised information stored in operational documents, electronic correspondence, and contractual files.
Finally, based on the criteria for administrative fines set out in [[Article 83 GDPR#2]], the Romanian DPA decided to fine the controller €10,000 (RON 53,370) for the breach of [[Article 32 GDPR#1b]] and [[Article 32 GDPR#2]].
